questions.question: Which pattern is most consistent with classic vascular claudication?
choices: Reproducible exertional calf discomfort relieved by rest
Sudden cold pulseless leg at rest
Pain only after touching a foot ulcer
Leg pain relieved only by antibiotics
questions.explanation: Classic claudication is exertional muscle discomfort that is reproducible and resolves with rest.

questions.question: What is the role of a resting ABI in a patient with suspected PAD?
choices: It helps establish the diagnosis when history or examination suggests PAD
It replaces examination and symptom history
It diagnoses every cause of leg pain
It is used only after amputation
questions.explanation: A resting ABI is recommended to help establish PAD in patients with suggestive history or examination findings.

questions.question: Which finding is most concerning for chronic limb-threatening ischemia?
choices: A nonhealing ischemic-appearing foot ulcer with rest pain
Stable calf soreness after unusual exercise
A normal foot examination
A resolved ankle sprain
questions.explanation: Ischemic rest pain, nonhealing wounds, and gangrene are CLTI features that require urgent limb-preservation evaluation.

questions.question: Which presentation requires emergency evaluation for possible acute limb ischemia?
choices: Sudden painful cool pulseless leg with new paresthesia
Chronic stable exertional discomfort
A scheduled podiatry visit
No change from baseline walking tolerance
questions.explanation: Sudden loss of perfusion with pain, coolness, pulse change, or neurologic symptoms can threaten limb viability.

questions.question: Why should PAD care include cardiovascular prevention?
choices: PAD is associated with increased MI, stroke, and cardiovascular risk
PAD affects only skin color
Exercise is never relevant
Foot care replaces cardiovascular care
questions.explanation: PAD is systemic atherosclerotic disease and carries elevated cardiovascular as well as limb risk.

questions.question: What is an appropriate longitudinal intervention for chronic symptomatic PAD?
choices: A structured exercise program with behavioral support when clinically appropriate
Avoiding all walking permanently
Ignoring tobacco exposure
Using wound care only when there is no wound
questions.explanation: Supervised or structured exercise can improve walking performance, function, and quality of life in chronic symptomatic PAD.

questions.question: Why should antithrombotic therapy be reconciled carefully in PAD?
choices: The appropriate regimen depends on indications, bleeding risk, AF, kidney function, procedures, and current guidance
All patients need every antithrombotic agent
OTC NSAIDs cannot affect bleeding risk
Medication history is unrelated to PAD care
questions.explanation: Antithrombotic decisions are individualized and can be altered by competing indications, bleeding risk, kidney function, and drug interactions.

questions.question: What should a focused PAD examination include?
choices: Both legs and feet, pulses, perfusion, skin/tissue, wounds, sensation, and footwear
Only a pulse in one foot
Only body weight
Only a fasting glucose value
questions.explanation: PAD assessment requires bilateral vascular and foot examination with attention to tissue and neurologic risk.

questions.question: What is an important foot-protection message for a patient with PAD and diabetes?
choices: Inspect feet regularly and report wounds, new pain, or color changes promptly
Treat footwear as unrelated to limb risk
Use thermal devices on numb feet
Wait until gangrene develops before seeking care
questions.explanation: Daily foot protection and early reporting of changes can help prevent tissue loss and amputation.

questions.question: What is the FNP-level PAD principle?
choices: Treat the leg symptom without considering vascular risk
Classify urgency, protect limb and cardiovascular health, and coordinate feasible long-term care
Assume all leg pain is PAD
Delay referral until walking is impossible
questions.explanation: High-quality PAD care combines accurate classification, limb-threat recognition, risk reduction, foot protection, and coordinated follow-up.
